opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's an interesting one, because looking back people tend to tell it as a clean story: AlexNet came out, everyone saw the numbers, and the field switched overnight. It wasn't quite like that.

At the time I was in Yann LeCun's lab at NYU, so we were already in the neural network camp. For us it was validation. Yann had been pushing convolutional nets for decades, and here was a result on the benchmark everyone cared about, with a margin that was hard to argue with. The error rate didn't drop by a point or two, it dropped by around ten. That's not noise.

The broader vision community was more mixed. A lot of very smart people had spent years building careful pipelines: SIFT features, HOG, Fisher vectors, spatial pyramids, deformable part models. There was real craft in that, and an understandable instinct to say, "Okay, this works on ImageNet classification, but is it general? Is it just a big dataset trick? Does it transfer to detection, segmentation, real problems?" Some of that skepticism was healthy. Some of it was just people not wanting to throw out what they'd built their careers on.

What really changed minds wasn't just the 2012 paper. It was the follow-up over the next year or two. People started pulling features off the penultimate layer of these networks, putting a linear classifier on top, and beating hand-engineered state of the art across a whole range of datasets. Then R-CNN showed the gains carried over to detection. Once you saw that over and over, it was very hard to stay on the sidelines.

The other piece people underappreciate is tooling. Alex's cuda-convnet was impressive, but it wasn't something most groups could just pick up. Getting GPUs, writing kernels, dealing with training instability, that was a real barrier. Part of why the transition took a couple of years is that the software had to catch up so normal researchers could actually run these experiments. That's a big part of what motivated me to work on frameworks like Torch and later PyTorch: the ideas were there, but the friction of trying them was holding people back.

So I'd say the response went from curiosity and skepticism, to grudging acceptance, to a pretty complete shift by around 2014. Looking back, it's one of the fastest paradigm changes I've seen in any field.

r001.rationale: The response says some skepticism about whether the results generalized was healthy.

r002.rationale: It contrasts neural-network proponents with the broader vision community, but does not say younger researchers were more receptive than established professors.

r003.rationale: It describes a pretty complete shift by around 2014, roughly two years after the 2012 results.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I actually had a front-row seat to this in a funny way, because in 2012 I was a grad student at NYU working with Yann, and we were essentially the people who had been saying for years that convnets would work if you just scaled them up. So when the AlexNet result came out, the reaction inside our lab was more like relief than surprise. Like, finally, somebody has the GPU implementation and the dataset at the same scale and it does the thing we always said it would do.

But the broader vision community was a different story. I think the honest answer is that a lot of people did not believe it at first, or they believed it but they didn't think it mattered. There was this whole generation of researchers who had built their careers on hand-engineered features, SIFT, HOG, the deformable parts model, all of that. And the dominant feeling was that these neural net people were just brute-forcing something that should be solved elegantly. I remember hearing things like, well, it's a black box, you can't understand what it's doing, so it doesn't count as science. And there was also a lot of skepticism about whether it would generalize beyond ImageNet. People thought it was a one-off on one benchmark.

What changed the tone was really the next year or two. Once Matt Zeiler and Rob Fergus did the deconvolution visualizations and showed that the network was learning things that looked like edges and textures and object parts, that gave people a kind of permission to accept it. And then as results kept coming, in detection, in segmentation, in face recognition, the holdouts started quietly switching over. By CVPR 2014 it was basically a stampede. Everyone had a convnet paper.

I'd say the thing that was slightly unfortunate was how much of the response was driven by sociology rather than science. The evidence was there in 2012. It took the community a couple of years to update, mostly because updating meant admitting that the thing you had spent a decade on was going to be irrelevant. That's a very human thing, I don't blame anyone for it. But it's a useful lesson. Whenever you see a result that looks too good, and it's coming from people you consider outsiders, it's worth asking whether your skepticism is about the evidence or about your identity.

r001.rationale: The response portrays initial skepticism as driven largely by career interests and sociology, and says the evidence was already there; it does not call the reaction healthy scientific skepticism.

r002.rationale: It does not compare younger researchers’ receptiveness with that of established professors.

r003.rationale: It says the tone changed over the next year or two and that by CVPR 2014 it was a “stampede” with everyone having a convnet paper, indicating broad acceptance within roughly two years.

astra-6.text:
I think the response was understandable. The computer vision community had spent years building up techniques and intuitions about what worked, and then Alex’s result came along and showed a huge improvement with a very different approach. You don’t immediately throw away everything you know because of one result. You ask, “Is this reproducible? What’s actually responsible for the improvement? Does it work beyond this benchmark?”

But there’s a difference between that kind of skepticism and dismissing the result because it doesn’t fit your view of the field. The productive response is to engage with it and test it. So I wouldn’t characterize the community as having one uniform reaction. A result like that challenges both technical assumptions and people’s investment in their existing work, and those things take time to disentangle.

r001.rationale: It describes the community’s skepticism as understandable and says the productive response is to test reproducibility and investigate the result.

r002.rationale: It does not compare younger researchers’ receptiveness with that of established professors.

r003.rationale: It gives no timeline for broad acceptance of neural networks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the community deserves a lot of credit for how quickly it responded. You had this result that challenged years of work on hand-designed features, and people could have spent a long time resisting it. Instead, a lot of researchers said, “Okay, this works much better. Let’s understand it and build on it.”

That doesn’t mean everyone was immediately convinced, but the field shifted remarkably quickly. To me, that willingness to change direction when the evidence changes is a real strength of the computer vision community.

r001.rationale: The response praises the community’s willingness to change direction, but describes resistance only as something that could have happened; it does not characterize actual initial skepticism as a healthy scientific reaction.

r002.rationale: It makes no distinction between younger researchers and established professors.

r003.rationale: It says the field shifted quickly, but gives no roughly two-year timeframe and does not state that the community broadly accepted neural networks.
